 Trump taps OMB deputy to lead GAO amid rushed selection process
 Eric Ueland would serve a 15-year term leading the congressional watchdog that has challenged the Trump administration's spending and workforce actions.
 Jory Heckman 
 | 
 November 16, 2026 06:08 PM ET
 Waste, Fraud & Abuse
 Jory Heckman 
 Senior Reporter 
 President Donald Trump is nominating a top budget official and close ally of Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought to lead the Government Accountability Office. Trump nominated OMB Deputy Director Eric Ueland to serve as comptroller general, a position that carries a 15-year term.
 Under  the current process , a commission of 10 senior lawmakers from both parties in the House and Senate recommends candidates to the president.
 The last time lawmakers vetted candidates for GAO’s top job in 2010, the congressional commission spent more than a year on its search. But last week, members of the commission were given 24-hours’ notice on a federal holiday to come up with at least three candidates. Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., is responsible for convening the commission.
 The committee is scheduled to hold a  confirmation hearing  for Ueland on Thursday, along with nine other nominees for a variety of posts. 
 The appointment comes as GAO has taken an increasingly active role in scrutinizing the Trump administration's actions. If confirmed by the Senate, Ueland would lead an agency responsible for monitoring cases of impoundment, where agencies withhold funding enacted by Congress. As of July 2025, GAO had opened at least 46 impoundment investigations and found in some cases that agencies had  violated the Impoundment Control Act. 
 Trump has said that he wants to challenge the law against impoundment, which he says is unconstitutional. Vought has declined to commit to adhering to that law when asked during congressional hearings .
 GAO has also studied the impact of the Trump administration’s federal workforce cuts – although agency heads have rebuffed those efforts . Ueland said in March that reducing the size of the federal government and its workforce remains “priority number one.” 
 Ueland said last week at an industry conference that the Trump administration’s reshaping of the federal government has been “long overdue.”
 Ueland has held other leadership positions during the Trump administration. He previously served as the acting administrator of the now-shuttered U.S. Agency for International Development and the acting director of the  Office of Government Ethics. 
 Senate Democrats quickly denounced the expedited process that led to Ueland’s nomination. 
 HSGAC Ranking Member Gary Peters, D-Mich., who serves on the commission that selects comptroller general candidates, said in a statement that Ueland’s nomination to GAO’s top job would compromise the agency’s role as a watchdog that serves Congress and helps root out fraud, waste and abuse.
 “President Trump’s nomination of Eric Ueland – and Congressional Republicans’ rubber stamp of this nomination in violation of longstanding bipartisan practice – only provides further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever,” Peters said. 
 Senate Appropriations Committee Vice Chairwoman Patty Murray, D-Wash., urged her Republican colleagues to “reject this outrageous nomination.” 
 “It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting new ways for this administration to defy Congress,” Murray said. “Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO.” 
 Henry Wray, a former GAO attorney who retired as its senior associate general counsel and who helped develop the 1980 law establishing the current comptroller general selection process, warned HSGAC leadership in a letter that the fast-tracking of Ueland’s nomination “violates both the letter and the spirit of the law and is fundamentally at odds with the deliberative, bipartisan process it requires.” 
 “These perversions of the statutory process clearly reveal the real objective underlying the exercise: to convert the Comptroller General into an agent of the administration rather than an agent of Congress in order to stymie rather than ensure rigorous, objective oversight of the executive branch. I urge you to reconsider,” Wray wrote. “Any Comptroller General who emerges from such a partisan, fractured, and legally dubious process will obviously lack broad-based credibility and thereby greatly diminish GAO and its usefulness to you as your watchdog agency. 
 A bipartisan coalition of civil society organizations also warned senators about “rushing through a nomination” for GAO’s top job. 
 Mark Lee Greenblatt, a former Interior Department inspector general fired by Trump last year , warned that Ueland, if confirmed, would lead an agency responsible for evaluating decisions in which he previously played a role. 
 “That raises serious questions about potential conflicts of interest and whether he could exercise the independence the position demands,” Greenblatt wrote. 
 “The Comptroller General must serve Congress and the American people, not the political interests of any administration or congressional majority. Rushing this appointment without a meaningful bipartisan search risks undermining confidence in the very institution Congress relies upon to hold the federal government accountable,” he added.
